title: Chapter LXI

teacherSummary.text: The epilogue: Jane and Bingley move near Pemberley; Kitty improves under her sisters' care; Mary stays home; Lydia and Wickham remain reckless. Lady Catherine eventually reconciles, and the Gardiners stay dear to the Darcys.

vocabulary.context: The congratulatory letter which Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage explained to her that, by his wife at least, if not by himself, such a hope was cherished.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “congratulatory”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Wanting in the qualities which affect the organs of taste
vocabulary.context: She was not of so ungovernable a temper as Lydia, and, removed from the influence of Lydia’s example, she became, by proper attention and management, less irritable, less ignorant, and less insipid.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “insipid”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Darcy, as well as Elizabeth, really loved them; and they were both ever sensible of the warmest gratitude towards the persons who, by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unit”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being near, or not remote
vocabulary.context: So near a vicinity to her mother and Meryton relations was not desirable even to his easy temper, or her affectionate heart.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “vicinity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To treat with tenderness and affection
vocabulary.context: The congratulatory letter which Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage explained to her that, by his wife at least, if not by himself, such a hope was cherished.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cherish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: They were always moving from place to place in quest of a cheap situation, and always spending more than they ought.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “spending”: pend (Latin pendere, "to hang, weigh") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Such relief, however, as it was in her power to afford, by the practice of what might be called economy in her own private expenses, she frequently sent them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “expense”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + pens (Latin pendere, "to weigh, pay"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Their manner of living, even when the restoration of peace dismissed them to a home, was unsettled in the extreme.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dismiss”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + miss (Latin mittere, "to send"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A light cape or short cloak of silk or lace worn by women in summer
vocabulary.context: With what delighted pride she afterwards visited Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “visite”: vis (Latin videre, "to see"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of following or going after
vocabulary.context: Mary was the only daughter who remained at home; and she was necessarily drawn from the pursuit of accomplishments by Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pursuit”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Novel epilogues often 'settle' each character's fate.

significance: The ending rewards growth and quietly punishes folly, affirming the novel's moral design.
discussionQuestions: Which ending surprised you most, and why?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

items.prompt: Where do Jane and Bingley eventually live?
Who improves under her sisters' care?
How do Lydia and Wickham end up?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LXI,” how does Austen show endings and futures? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LXI, how does Austen develop the idea of endings and futures? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LXI develops the idea of endings and futures. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LXI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of endings and futures. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LXI suggests about endings and futures. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LXI to complicate the reader's understanding of endings and futures. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LXI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of endings and futures responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LXI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of endings and futures follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LXI and its treatment of endings and futures. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LXI as evidence for a larger claim about endings and futures in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LXI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of endings and futures. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Happy for all her maternal feelings was the day on which Mrs. Bennet got rid of her two most deserving daughters. With what delighted pride she afterwards visited Mrs. Bingley and talked of Mrs. Darcy may be guessed. I wish I could say, for the sake of her family, that the accomplishment of her earnest desire in the establishment of so many of her children, produced so happy an effect as to make her a sensible, amiable, well-informed woman for the rest of her life; though perhaps it was lucky for her husband, who might not have relished domestic felicity in so unusual a form, that she still was occasionally nervous and invariably silly.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter LXI”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Which ending surprised you most, and why? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are congratulatory, insipid, uniting, vicinity, cherished. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “The congratulatory letter which Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage explained to her that, by his wife at least, if not by himself, such a hope was cherished.” Webster's says: Expressive of sympathetic joy. Now the word history: “congratulatory”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ory (Latin -orius, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “insipid”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “unit”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Novel epilogues often 'settle' each character's fate. Why does this chapter matter? The ending rewards growth and quietly punishes folly, affirming the novel's moral design. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to endings and futures.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

With what delighted pride she afterwards visited Mrs. Bingley and talked of Mrs. Darcy may be guessed. I wish I could say, for the sake of her family, that the accomplishment of her earnest desire in the establishment of so many of her children, produced so happy an effect as to make her a sensible, amiable, well-informed woman for the rest of her life; though perhaps it was lucky for her husband, who might not have relished domestic felicity in so unusual a form, that she still was occasionally nervous and invariably silly.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LXI,” how does Austen show endings and futures? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about endings and futures, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes endings and futures. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
